Chapter One: The World Divided—Life Under Colonial Rule
Imagine waking up every morning in a place where your world is split clean down the middle. On one side, you see wide streets, parks that are always tidy, and homes that almost shine with comfort and ease. But take a few steps in the other direction, and it’s a completely different story—narrow, tangled alleys, dust swirling through the air, and houses patched together from whatever materials folks could find.
In this world, these two groups hardly ever mix. Unless, of course, it’s when one is serving the other. This isn’t just a bad day—it’s the everyday reality for so many people living under colonial rule. Invisible lines carve up their lives, making some feel privileged, while others are made to feel less than human.
For people living in the colonized zone, life is a constant reminder of all that’s been taken away. Picture a shopkeeper, watching shipments of goods leave the country, fully aware that any profits will never make their way back to his community. Kids grow up hearing stories—stories about lost lands and traditions that people now mock. Even the air feels heavy, thick with the knowledge that every rule was written by someone else, and never for their benefit.
On the colonizer’s side, there’s order and privilege. For everyone else, there’s just scarcity and a constant sense of suspicion. The police and military are always there—not to keep people safe, but to make sure those lines stay exactly where they are. Most people in these neighborhoods learn early on that staying safe means keeping quiet and following orders. Any hint of resistance? That’s met with harsh, sometimes brutal, punishment.
But if you look beneath the surface, you’ll find that frustration is always simmering. Every daily humiliation—being spoken down to, blocked from opportunities, or watching your culture get dismissed—leaves scars that don’t easily fade. Over the years, these wounds start to shape how people see themselves and each other. Some start to believe the lies they hear about their worth. Others, though, quietly hold onto a deep sense of anger and a hope for something different.
And it’s not just about what people have or don’t have. The colonized are made to feel invisible—their histories erased, their languages mocked. Imagine a teacher in a rural school, forced to teach in a foreign language, watching her students struggle to find the right words. Elders remember a time before these lines existed, but their memories are fading, slowly being replaced by the colonizer’s version of history.
In this divided world, violence is always close by. You see it in how the police patrol the streets, in the fear that keeps people quiet, and in the silent despair that settles over families. For most, the idea of fighting back just feels impossible—the colonizer’s power looks absolute, and the risks of resistance are dangerously high.
Still, hope has a way of sticking around. In whispered conversations and secret gatherings, people share dreams of a different future. They remember that life wasn’t always split like this. And as the pressure builds, it’s only a matter of time before things start to change. The real question is—when, and how?
